finfet-001.question: Which correctly describes the structure of a FinFET?
choices: The gate wraps around a fin-shaped channel on three sides
A planar gate covers only the top of the channel
Metal contacts the channel directly with no gate insulator
finfet-001.explanation: A FinFET stands silicon up as a fin a few to over ten nm wide and tens of nm tall, with the gate wrapping both sidewalls and the top. Gate control from three sides suppresses short-channel effects better than planar devices, cutting off-state leakage, and the vertical dimension provides current-carrying width in a small footprint. It became the advanced-logic standard from the 22 nm generation.

finfet-002.question: Which correctly describes a GAA (gate-all-around) transistor?
choices: The gate covers only the top of the channel
The gate surrounds the entire perimeter of the channel, such as nanosheets
It has no gate and operates with only a source and drain
finfet-002.explanation: A gate-all-around (GAA) transistor stacks several channels shaped as sheets a few nm thick (nanosheets) or wires, each fully surrounded by the gate. Control from all sides is even stronger than in a FinFET, suppressing short-channel effects down to shorter gate lengths. Samsung adopted it at 3 nm (2022), TSMC at 2 nm and Intel at 18A, making it the successor standard to the FinFET.

finfet-003.question: Which describes a short-channel effect in MOSFETs?
choices: Shortening the gate makes the gate capacitance infinite
Shortening the gate always doubles the channel mobility
Shortening the gate lowers the threshold voltage and increases off-state leakage
finfet-003.explanation: As gate length shrinks, the source and drain depletion regions become relatively large and control part of the channel charge instead of the gate. Consequences include threshold roll-off, drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL), degraded subthreshold swing and rising off-state leakage. Device characteristics also become highly sensitive to small process variations in gate length.

finfet-004.question: What is the main reason for using high-k (high-dielectric-constant) materials for the gate insulator?
choices: A material with a high dielectric constant gives large gate capacitance with a thicker physical film, suppressing tunneling current
To reduce wiring resistance
To eliminate the gate insulator itself
finfet-004.explanation: Below about 1.2 nm, SiO2 gate leakage from tunneling multiplies several-fold with every 0.1 nm of thinning. Hafnium-based oxides with relative permittivity of about 20–25 allow several times the physical thickness at the same capacitance, cutting leakage by orders of magnitude. Because high-k films pin the threshold with polysilicon gates (Fermi-level pinning), they are paired with metal gates, in use since the 45 nm generation (2007).

finfet-005.question: What is the main purpose of applying strain (stress) to a transistor's channel?
choices: To make the threshold voltage 0 V
To increase carrier mobility and drive current
To reduce gate capacitance
finfet-005.explanation: Straining silicon alters its band structure, reducing effective mass and scattering to boost mobility. Tensile strain along the current direction helps nMOS, compressive strain helps pMOS; methods include embedding SiGe in pMOS source/drain regions and capping nMOS with tensile nitride films. Introduced around the 90 nm generation (2003), strain became a pillar of performance improvement alongside scaling.

finfet-006.question: Which correctly describes EOT (equivalent oxide thickness)?
choices: The thickness of an SiO2 film that would give the same gate capacitance as a gate insulator such as a high-k film
The actual physical thickness of the gate insulator
The thickness of the wiring layers
finfet-006.explanation: EOT expresses a gate dielectric's capacitance as the thickness of SiO2 (relative permittivity 3.9) that would give the same value: EOT = physical thickness × 3.9/ε. A high-k film with ε = 20 needs about 5 nm physically for 1 nm EOT. Advanced devices reach about 0.8–1 nm EOT including the interfacial layer. Measured electrical thickness (CET) is somewhat larger because of inversion-layer quantum effects and similar contributions.

finfet-007.question: Which correctly describes the SOI (silicon on insulator) structure?
choices: A transistor structure with no gate insulator
A structure in which transistors are built in a thin silicon layer on a buried oxide
A structure with two chips stacked
finfet-007.explanation: SOI builds transistors in a thin silicon layer on top of a buried oxide (BOX) within the wafer. Isolation from the substrate lowers junction capacitance and leakage and eliminates latch-up. SOI wafers are made by methods such as Smart Cut, which bonds an oxidized wafer to another and splits off a thin layer. SOI is widely used for RF switches (RF-SOI) and low-power FD-SOI logic.

finfet-008.question: Which correctly describes DIBL (drain-induced barrier lowering)?
choices: The gate insulator breaks down over time
Metal atoms in wiring migrate due to current
The higher the drain voltage, the lower the potential barrier at the source, lowering the threshold voltage
finfet-008.explanation: With a short gate, the drain's field reaches toward the source and lowers the source-channel potential barrier. Threshold voltage therefore falls as drain voltage rises, increasing off-state leakage. DIBL is quoted as threshold shift per volt of drain bias (mV/V), kept to a few tens of mV/V or less in advanced transistors. In amplifiers it also lowers output resistance.

finfet-009.question: How is the effective channel width of a FinFET adjusted?
choices: By changing the number of fins, so the width takes discrete values
By changing the gate voltage
It can be set to any continuous value, as in planar transistors
finfet-009.explanation: In a FinFET, fin height and width are fixed by the process, so channel width is adjusted only by the number of fins—a discrete quantity ("width quantization"). This makes it hard to set fine current ratios in analog circuits or tune the strength ratios among SRAM cell transistors, constraining design. Nanosheet GAA devices relax this limitation.

finfet-010.question: Which correctly describes the CFET (complementary FET), researched as the structure to follow GAA?
choices: It simplifies the structure by eliminating the gate electrode
It stacks nMOS and pMOS vertically to reduce cell area
It returns transistors to a planar structure
finfet-010.explanation: A CFET stacks the nMOS and pMOS nanosheets of a CMOS circuit vertically rather than placing them side by side, potentially building the same function in nearly half the area. Forming different materials and gate metals for n and p in the stack is complex, and routing connections to the upper and lower devices is challenging. Development targets practical use in the 2030s.

finfet-011.question: In high-k/metal gate transistors, which is one of the main ways to adjust the threshold voltage?
choices: Choosing the work function of the metal used for the gate electrode
Changing the wafer diameter
Changing the package material
finfet-011.explanation: In metal-gate transistors, the gate metal's work function sets the flat-band voltage and thus the threshold. nMOS needs a work function near the conduction band (about 4.1 eV, e.g., TiAl) and pMOS one near the valence band (about 5.1 eV, e.g., TiN). Combining thin metal layers a few nm thick in different stacks and thicknesses produces multiple thresholds for high-speed and low-leakage devices.

finfet-012.question: Which correctly describes the gate-last (replacement metal gate) process?
choices: The metal gate is made first, and then all high-temperature steps are performed
The transistor is first formed with a dummy gate, and after high-temperature steps the dummy is removed and replaced with a metal gate
A transistor without a gate is made
finfet-012.explanation: High-temperature steps such as source/drain activation anneals (around 1000 °C) can shift the work function of high-k films and metal gates. In a gate-last flow, polysilicon dummy gates go through the hot steps first; then the dielectric is planarized to expose the dummies, which are removed, and high-k and metal gates fill the resulting trenches. Intel adopted it at 45 nm, and it is now mainstream.

finfet-013.question: What is an advantage of fully depleted SOI (FD-SOI) transistors?
choices: The silicon layer can be thick and heavily doped
No gate electrode is needed
The channel can be lightly doped, threshold voltage variation is reduced, and the threshold is easy to adjust with body bias
finfet-013.explanation: In FD-SOI, an extremely thin silicon layer of about 5–7 nm is fully depleted, so short-channel effects are controlled without channel doping and random-dopant variability is small. Applying voltage from the substrate through a thin buried oxide (about 20 nm) shifts the threshold dynamically, making FD-SOI attractive for low-voltage, low-power IoT, automotive and RF applications.

finfet-014.question: In very small transistors, what is the phenomenon called in which the threshold voltage varies because of statistical variation in the number and positions of dopant atoms in the channel?
choices: Random dopant fluctuation (RDF)
Electromigration
Time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB)
finfet-014.explanation: As transistors shrink, their channels contain only tens to hundreds of dopant atoms, and random variation in their number and placement scatters threshold voltage by tens of mV. Variation scales roughly as 1/√(gate area) (Pelgrom's law) and is especially troublesome in circuits like SRAM that use many minimum-size devices. FinFETs and FD-SOI, which allow undoped channels, are advantageous here.

finfet-015.question: Compared with FinFETs, what is a design advantage of nanosheet GAA transistors?
choices: Channel width can only be changed by the number of fins
Drive current can be adjusted more flexibly by changing the nanosheet width
Gate length does not affect transistor characteristics
finfet-015.explanation: A FinFET's channel width can change only by fin count, but in nanosheet GAA the stacked sheets' width (e.g., 15–50 nm) can be varied continuously in layout. Wide sheets suit high-performance cells and narrow ones suit low-power logic and SRAM, giving flexible control of drive current and capacitance. The all-around gate also resists short-channel effects, delivering more current than a FinFET in the same footprint.

finfet-016.question: Which technique, used to make the thin fins of FinFETs, uses sidewall spacers to create patterns finer than the lithography limit?
choices: SADP/SAQP (self-aligned double/quadruple patterning)
OPC
CMP
finfet-016.explanation: SADP coats a mandrel pattern with a conformal film (e.g., by ALD), forms sidewall spacers, then removes the mandrel, doubling line density. SAQP repeats this to quadruple it. Because line width is set by film thickness rather than exposure, variation is small, and fins and wires finer than ArF immersion's limit (about 80 nm pitch) become possible. Even with EUV, these techniques are combined for the tightest pitches.

finfet-017.question: In manufacturing nanosheet GAA transistors, why is only the SiGe selectively removed from stacked alternating Si and SiGe layers?
choices: To make the transistor lighter
So that the gate insulator and gate electrode can be filled into the gaps, surrounding each Si nanosheet with the gate
Because SiGe does not conduct electricity
finfet-017.explanation: Nanosheet GAA starts from an epitaxial stack of alternating Si and SiGe (about 25–30% Ge). After the dummy gate is removed, SiGe is etched away with high selectivity, leaving the Si sheets suspended. Filling the gaps with high-k and metal gate by ALD wraps each sheet on all sides. Selective etching that removes only SiGe without damaging the sheets is the manufacturing key.

finfet-018.question: What is the cause of self-heating, which tends to be a problem in FinFETs and SOI transistors?
choices: The transistor gets too cold
No current flows at all
The channel is thin or surrounded by insulators, so heat generated cannot easily escape to the substrate
finfet-018.explanation: Narrow structures like fins, or devices surrounded by low-thermal-conductivity oxide (SiO2 conducts about 1/100 as well as silicon), shed heat poorly to the substrate, so channels can run tens of degrees hotter than their surroundings. Higher temperature lowers mobility and current and accelerates electromigration in nearby wiring and device degradation, so it must be accounted for in reliability assessment and circuit design.

finfet-019.question: In highly scaled transistors, which factors are becoming increasingly important limits on performance?
choices: Parasitic resistance of source, drain and contacts, and parasitic capacitance around the gate
Wafer diameter
Package color
finfet-019.explanation: As transistors shrink, source/drain and contact resistance grow relative to channel resistance and can approach half of total on-resistance in advanced nodes. Gate-to-contact spacing shrinks to around ten nm, increasing parasitic capacitance. Performance gains therefore now come largely from extrinsic improvements: better contact materials, air-gap or low-k spacers, and backside power delivery.

finfet-020.question: Which correctly describes materials such as molybdenum disulfide (MoS2), researched as channel materials for future ultra-small transistors?
choices: They are metals a few mm thick
They are two-dimensional materials that act as semiconductors even a few atomic layers thick
They are insulators that do not conduct electricity
finfet-020.explanation: Transition-metal dichalcogenides such as MoS2 remain semiconducting even as a single layer three atoms thick (about 0.65 nm). With no dangling bonds on their surfaces, they keep reasonable mobility when thinned. Silicon below a few nm suffers severe surface-roughness scattering, so 2D materials are candidates for ultra-thin channels beyond GAA, though uniform large-area growth and low-resistance contacts remain challenges.

finfet-021.question: What is the main purpose of growing raised crystal on the fins in the source and drain of a FinFET by epitaxial growth?
choices: To make the transistor emit light
To lengthen the gate
To reduce parasitic resistance and apply strain to the channel
finfet-021.explanation: Fins are only a few nm wide, so source/drain resistance would be high and contact area small. Epitaxially growing diamond-shaped raised crystals enlarges the cross-section, lowering resistance and easing contact formation. pMOS uses Ge-rich SiGe and nMOS uses heavily phosphorus-doped SiP; their lattice mismatch also strains the channel to boost mobility.

finfet-022.question: What is the basic way to reduce metal-semiconductor contact resistance?
choices: Heavily dope the semiconductor at the contact to thin the barrier and make tunneling easier
Make the semiconductor at the contact extremely lightly doped
Insert a thick oxide between the metal and semiconductor
finfet-022.explanation: A Schottky barrier forms at metal-semiconductor interfaces. Raising semiconductor doping above 10²⁰ cm⁻³ thins the barrier to a few nm or less so carriers tunnel through easily, lowering contact resistance. Silicide interfaces such as titanium silicide, low-barrier materials and enlarged contact areas are also used, as advanced nodes demand specific contact resistivities around 10⁻⁹ Ω·cm².

finfet-023.question: Which is considered to show the real degree of logic scaling better than the process generation (node) name?
choices: The wafer diameter
Actual dimensions such as gate pitch (CPP) and minimum metal pitch
The chip's selling price
finfet-023.explanation: Through the 1990s node names roughly matched physical dimensions such as gate length, but since FinFETs names like "3 nm" merely denote a generation of performance and density; actual gate lengths exceed ten-odd nm. Real density is compared using contacted poly pitch (CPP, just under 50 nm at 3 nm), minimum metal pitch (in the 20 nm range), SRAM cell area and transistor density per mm².

finfet-024.question: Which devices are being researched with the aim of breaking the 60 mV/dec subthreshold swing barrier?
choices: Diodes
Thyristors
Tunnel FETs and negative-capacitance FETs
finfet-024.explanation: Conventional MOSFETs rely on carriers thermally surmounting a barrier, so at room temperature they cannot switch more steeply than 60 mV/dec, a barrier to lowering supply voltage. Tunnel FETs conduct by band-to-band tunneling between source and channel, escaping the thermal distribution, while negative-capacitance FETs use a ferroelectric's negative capacitance to amplify gate voltage internally—both aiming below the limit. Low on-current is among the remaining challenges.

finfet-025.question: In nanosheet GAA, what is the main role of the insulator (inner spacer) placed between the gate and the source/drain between the sheets?
choices: To reduce parasitic capacitance between the gate and source/drain and prevent shorts
To make the channel emit light
To amplify current
finfet-025.explanation: In nanosheet GAA, the gate fills the gaps between sheets and faces the source/drain only a few nm away. Inner spacers are formed by recessing the ends of the SiGe layers and filling the cavities with a dielectric such as nitride, reducing gate-to-source/drain capacitance and preventing shorts. They also protect the source/drain as an etch stop when the SiGe is removed.

finfet-026.question: When standard cell height is expressed in the number of routing tracks, what is the effect of reducing the number of tracks?
choices: Cell area shrinks and density increases
Cell area grows
The number of wires increases
finfet-026.explanation: Standard-cell height is expressed in tracks—the number of minimum-pitch wires that fit over it; six tracks at a 28 nm metal pitch is about 170 nm. Fewer tracks mean shorter cells and smaller circuit area. Advanced nodes have gone from about 7.5T to 6T to 5T, but less routing room and fewer fins (or sheets) per device raise congestion and reduce drive strength.

finfet-027.question: What is the purpose of using several types of transistors with different threshold voltages on the same chip?
choices: To decorate the chip
To use low-threshold transistors where speed is needed and high-threshold ones where leakage should be low, balancing performance and power
To make the threshold voltage unmeasurable
finfet-027.explanation: Low-threshold transistors are fast but leaky—lowering Vth by 0.1 V raises leakage by more than tenfold. Chips therefore offer several flavors (LVT, SVT, HVT) and use low thresholds only on timing-critical paths, high thresholds elsewhere. Design tools swap cells automatically based on timing analysis, preserving performance while sharply cutting standby power.

finfet-028.question: Which technique covers the gate with insulator so that a slightly misaligned contact does not short to the gate?
choices: LDD
TSV
Self-aligned contact (SAC)
finfet-028.explanation: Capping the gate's top and sides with nitride means that if a contact etch lands over the gate due to misalignment, it stops on the nitride—etched far more slowly than oxide—and never reaches the gate. Self-aligned contacts remove the margin otherwise reserved for overlay error, tightening gate-to-contact spacing, and lead to techniques such as contact-over-active-gate (COAG) that further shrink cells.

finfet-029.question: Why are SiGe and germanium considered or adopted instead of silicon as pMOS channel materials?
choices: Because their hole mobility is high
Because their electron mobility is very low
Because the materials are cheap
finfet-029.explanation: Germanium and SiGe have lighter hole effective mass and higher hole mobility than silicon, increasing pMOS drive current. SiGe behaves much like silicon and integrates readily into existing flows, and its band offset helps tune threshold voltage together with metal gates, so advanced processes use SiGe pMOS channels. Pure germanium channels are also under research.

finfet-030.question: Which 3D integration method builds transistor layers one after another on the wafer, without bonding chips?
choices: 2.5D integration
Monolithic 3D integration (sequential 3D integration)
SiP
finfet-030.explanation: Monolithic (sequential) 3D integration builds a second transistor layer on top of the first by forming or transferring a thin semiconductor layer. Tiers connect through vias tens of nm in size—over ten thousand times denser than TSV-based die stacking. Processing the upper tier must stay below about 500 °C to avoid damaging the lower devices and wiring. CFETs built sequentially are one form of this approach.

finfet-031.question: Which company and generation first put FinFETs (called Tri-Gate by Intel) into volume-production logic products?
choices: Intel's 22 nm generation (around 2011–2012)
TSMC's 90 nm generation (around 2004)
Samsung's 2 nm generation (around 2025)
finfet-031.explanation: Intel introduced FinFETs (which it called Tri-Gate) at 22 nm, shipping them from Ivy Bridge in 2012 and claiming about half the power at the same performance. TSMC and Samsung followed at 16/14 nm, completing the shift from planar transistors. The FinFET concept was published in 1999 by Chenming Hu and colleagues at UC Berkeley.
choiceNotes: Correct. Intel was first to adopt them in volume at 22 nm.
The 90 nm generation was the era of planar transistors.
At the 2 nm generation, the industry is moving to GAA.

finfet-032.question: Which company and generation were first to announce volume production of GAA (nanosheet) transistors?
choices: Intel's 45 nm generation
Samsung's 3 nm generation (2022)
TSMC's 28 nm generation
finfet-032.explanation: Samsung announced in 2022 that it had begun mass production of GAA transistors (branded MBCFET) at 3 nm. TSMC adopted GAA at its 2 nm node (N2) and Intel at 18A (RibbonFET), with volume production ramping from around 2025. Flexible nanosheet widths and pairing with new technologies such as backside power delivery are key to GAA's performance gains.
choiceNotes: The 45 nm generation introduced high-k/metal gates into planar transistors.
Correct. Samsung was first to announce volume production, at 3 nm.
The 28 nm generation used planar transistors.

finfet-033.question: What is the main purpose of scaling transistors down?
choices: To always increase the chip's power consumption
To make each transistor larger and heavier
To integrate more transistors in the same area and improve performance, power and cost
finfet-033.explanation: Smaller transistors pack more circuitry into the same area, lowering cost per transistor; reduced capacitance also brings speed and power benefits. Improving these three together—PPA: performance, power and area—is the purpose of scaling. Density doubled roughly every two years in line with Moore's law, but rising manufacturing costs have recently slowed the decline in cost per transistor.
choiceNotes: Scaling generally reduces the power per circuit.
Scaling means making transistors smaller.
Correct. Higher integration improves performance, power and cost.

finfet-034.question: What does "nanosheet" refer to in a nanosheet GAA transistor?
choices: A sheet-like film that protects the chip
A thin, plate-shaped silicon channel a few nanometers thick, stacked vertically
A thin metal plate used as the gate insulator
finfet-034.explanation: A nanosheet is a thin plate of silicon channel about 5 nm thick and over ten to several tens of nm wide; about three are stacked vertically, each wrapped by the gate. It resembles a FinFET fin laid on its side and stacked, with sheet width setting the current. Sheets are spaced about 10 nm apart, requiring advanced deposition to fill the gaps with gate dielectric and metal.
choiceNotes: It is not a protective film.
Correct. It is a stack of thin, plate-shaped channels.
The gate insulator is an insulator such as high-k, not a metal plate.

finfet-035.question: What does the "k" in "high-k gate dielectric" represent?
choices: Crystal hardness
Thermal conductivity
Relative permittivity (dielectric constant)
finfet-035.explanation: The "k" in high-k is the relative permittivity; materials above SiO2's (about 3.9) are called high-k. Representative examples are HfO2 (about 20–25) and HfSiON, which provide large gate capacitance with physically thicker films. Higher-k materials tend to have smaller bandgaps, so selection balances leakage. Between interconnects, by contrast, low-k materials are used to reduce capacitance.
choiceNotes: It does not stand for hardness.
It does not stand for thermal conductivity.
Correct. k represents the relative permittivity.

finfet-036.question: For a FinFET whose fin is 50 nm tall and 6 nm wide, which is closest to the effective channel width per fin (the perimeter wrapped by the gate)?
choices: 106 nm
6 nm
56 nm
finfet-036.explanation: The gate wraps both sidewalls and the top, so each fin's effective width is 2 × height + width = 2 × 50 + 6 = 106 nm. With a 30 nm fin pitch, that is more than three times the width a planar device gets in the same footprint, and taller fins add current without adding area. Very tall, thin fins may collapse or vary in shape, so heights around 50 nm are used.
choiceNotes: Correct. 2 × 50 + 6 = 106 nm.
6 nm is only the fin width and ignores the sidewalls.
56 nm counts only one sidewall and the top.

finfet-037.question: To adequately suppress short-channel effects in a FinFET, what is generally required of the fin width?
choices: It can be chosen independently of the gate length
Make it much wider than the gate length
Make it thinner than the gate length
finfet-037.explanation: The thinner the fin, the better the gates on both sides reach its center, suppressing leakage through regions far from the gate. Fin width should be roughly half to equal the gate length or less, about 5–7 nm in advanced nodes. Making fins too thin, however, introduces threshold shifts from quantum confinement, mobility loss from surface scattering and process variability.
choiceNotes: Fin width strongly affects suppression of short-channel effects.
Too thick a fin leaves the center uncontrolled by the gate, increasing leakage.
Correct. A thin fin strengthens gate control.

finfet-038.question: In high-k/metal gate transistors, why is a very thin layer such as SiO2 often placed between the silicon and the high-k film (such as hafnium oxide)?
choices: To preserve the quality of the silicon interface and limit effects such as mobility degradation
To increase the gate capacitance
To lower the resistance of the metal gate
finfet-038.explanation: High-k films placed directly on silicon degrade channel mobility through interface defects plus charges and lattice vibrations in the high-k layer (remote phonons). A thin interfacial layer (IL) of SiO2 or similar, about 0.5–1 nm, preserves a good interface. Because this low-k layer accounts for much of the EOT, thinning it as much as possible is key to reducing EOT.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is a layer for preserving interface quality.
The interfacial layer has low permittivity, so it actually lowers the gate capacitance.
It is unrelated to the gate electrode's resistance.

finfet-039.question: Why have III-V compound semiconductors such as InGaAs been researched as future nMOS channel materials?
choices: Because they can be manufactured more cheaply than silicon
Because their electron mobility is far higher than silicon's
Because their band gap is larger than silicon's, giving less leakage
finfet-039.explanation: III-V compounds such as InGaAs have electron mobilities several times silicon's or more, promising high current at low voltage. Yet defects from growth on silicon, difficulty forming good gate-dielectric interfaces, a low density of states that limits inversion charge, poor hole mobility and cost have kept them out of mass-produced logic.
choiceNotes: Compound semiconductors tend to cost more to manufacture than silicon.
Correct. The reason is their very high electron mobility.
InGaAs has a smaller band gap than silicon, which tends to increase leakage.

finfet-040.question: Which correctly describes the transistor performance metric "Ion/Ioff ratio"?
choices: The ratio of on-state current to off-state leakage current; the larger, the better the switch
The ratio of gate length to gate width
The ratio of supply voltage to threshold voltage
finfet-040.explanation: The Ion/Ioff ratio compares on-state current to off-state leakage, about 10⁴–10⁶ in advanced logic; higher means a better switch that is fast yet leaks little in standby. Lowering supply voltage forces a trade-off: keep Vth and lose Ion, or lower Vth and raise Ioff. FinFETs and GAA, with steeper subthreshold swings, deliver more Ion at the same Ioff.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is the ratio of on-current to off-current.
It is not a ratio of dimensions.
It is not a ratio of voltages.

finfet-041.question: How did the subthreshold swing (SS) generally change with the move from planar transistors to FinFETs?
choices: It fell below the theoretical limit of about 60 mV/dec
It approached (decreased toward) the theoretical limit of about 60 mV/dec
It increased, making the device harder to turn off
finfet-041.explanation: Subthreshold swing S = (kT/q)·ln10·(1 + Cd/Cox) approaches the ~60 mV/dec limit as non-gate capacitances (such as depletion) diminish. Scaled planar transistors had degraded to 80–100 mV/dec, but FinFETs, controlling the channel from three sides, improved to about 65–70 mV/dec. As long as devices operate by thermionic emission, however, they cannot go below 60 mV/dec.
choiceNotes: Conventional MOSFETs cannot go below 60 mV/dec because of the thermal limit.
Correct. Stronger gate control brings it closer to the limit.
SS improves (decreases) in FinFETs.

finfet-042.question: As physical scaling becomes harder, what is the practice of considering design and process technology together to optimize area and performance called?
choices: Wafer-level test
Moore's law
DTCO (design-technology co-optimization)
finfet-042.explanation: DTCO (design-technology co-optimization) develops transistor and interconnect process technology together with standard-cell and SRAM design rules to improve area, performance and power—for example, removing fins to shorten cells, or burying power rails or moving them to the backside to free routing. With dimensional shrinking alone no longer enough, it has become a major pillar of density scaling at advanced nodes.
choiceNotes: Wafer-level test means testing chips while still on the wafer.
Moore's law is an empirical rule about integration density, not the name of a practice.
Correct. Design and process are optimized together.

finfet-043.question: In nanosheet GAA transistors now in production, how many nanosheets are typically stacked in one transistor?
choices: About 3
About 100
finfet-043.explanation: Current nanosheet GAA devices typically stack about three sheets. More sheets add current per footprint, but taller stacks make source/drain epitaxy and filling the inter-sheet gaps with gate harder, and lower sheets suffer more parasitic resistance and capacitance. Added capacitance also hurts power more than it helps speed, so sheet count is a balance of benefit versus difficulty.
choiceNotes: A single sheet would forgo the current gain from stacking.
Correct. About three is typical.
Stacking 100 sheets is not realistic for logic transistors.

finfet-044.question: Which structure places nMOS and pMOS nanosheets close together on either side of a thin insulating wall to reduce cell area?
choices: FD-SOI
Planar MOSFET
Forksheet FET
finfet-044.explanation: A forksheet FET places nMOS and pMOS nanosheets on either side of a dielectric wall roughly ten-odd nm thick, forming a fork-tine shape. Standard GAA needs tens of nm between n and p devices, but the wall lets them sit much closer, shrinking standard cells and SRAM. Unlike full GAA, the gate wraps each sheet on three sides. It is a candidate generation between GAA and CFET.
choiceNotes: FD-SOI is a planar structure with a thin silicon layer on an insulator.
A planar device is the conventional structure with a flat channel.
Correct. n and p sheets sit on either side of a dielectric wall.

finfet-045.question: What is the state called in which the channel is so short that carriers travel from source to drain almost without scattering?
choices: Ballistic transport
Diffusive transport
Hopping transport
finfet-045.explanation: When channel length becomes comparable to or shorter than the carrier mean free path (about 10–20 nm for electrons in silicon at room temperature), carriers cross from source to drain with little scattering—ballistic transport. Current is then governed not by mobility but by the injection velocity from source into channel. Even fully ballistic devices have nonzero resistance: a quantum contact resistance set by quantum mechanics remains.
choiceNotes: Correct. Carriers pass through without scattering.
Diffusive transport is ordinary conduction with repeated scattering.
Hopping transport is carriers jumping between localized states, seen in amorphous materials and the like.

finfet-046.question: Which transistor has a source, channel and drain of the same conductivity type and doping, with no PN junctions?
choices: Bipolar transistor
IGBT
Junctionless transistor
finfet-046.explanation: A junctionless transistor dopes a thin silicon nanowire uniformly and heavily from source to drain and turns off by depleting the channel from the surrounding gate—essentially a gate-pinched resistor. With no need for abrupt PN junctions over nanometer distances, it scales easily; it was reported in 2010. Heavy channel doping lowers mobility, however, and variations in cross-section cause large threshold variability.
choiceNotes: A bipolar transistor has two PN junctions.
An IGBT has a structure with multiple PN junctions.
Correct. It is a transistor without PN junctions.

finfet-047.question: In FinFETs built on bulk substrates, what is the purpose of a heavily doped layer at the base of the fin (the part the gate controls poorly)?
choices: To suppress punch-through leakage flowing through the lower part of the fin
To lower the gate resistance
To make the fin taller
finfet-047.explanation: In bulk FinFETs, the fin base is not surrounded by the gate, so current can leak between source and drain beneath the channel. A heavily doped layer of the opposite type at the fin base (a punch-through stopper) blocks this path. The challenge is confining it sharply to that depth without doping the channel itself. SOI substrates provide oxide isolation instead, at higher wafer cost.
choiceNotes: Correct. It suppresses leakage under the fin.
It is unrelated to the gate electrode's resistance.
It is not a layer for changing fin height.

finfet-048.question: Which correctly describes the "scale length (natural length) λ" used to estimate the severity of short-channel effects?
choices: The length of the gate wiring
A measure of how far the drain potential's influence extends into the channel; if the gate length is much longer than λ, short-channel effects are small
Exactly the same value as the fin height
finfet-048.explanation: The scale length λ estimates the distance over which the drain's potential decays exponentially into the channel; for planar devices λ ≈ √((εSi/εox)·tox·tSi), set by oxide and channel thickness. Gate lengths about 5–10 times λ keep short-channel effects small. Structures with more gated surfaces—double gate, tri-gate, then GAA—have smaller λ and scale to shorter gate lengths.
choiceNotes: It does not represent a wiring length.
Correct. It measures how far the drain's influence reaches.
It is a different quantity from the fin height.

finfet-049.question: What is an effect of quantum confinement when fins or nanosheets are thinned to a few nanometers?
choices: The effective band gap increases and the threshold voltage shifts (thickness variation becomes threshold voltage variation)
The charge of the electron increases
Silicon turns into a metal
finfet-049.explanation: At channel thicknesses of a few nm, electron energies quantize into discrete subbands, lifting the lowest one above the conduction-band edge and widening the effective band gap. The shift scales inversely with thickness squared and grows rapidly as the body thins, so at about 2–3 nm a difference of a single atomic layer (about 0.3 nm) can move threshold voltage by ten-odd to tens of mV. Precise control of fin and nanosheet thickness is therefore essential.
choiceNotes: Correct. The effective band gap grows and the threshold voltage changes.
The charge of a single electron does not change.
Silicon does not become a metal.

finfet-050.question: In a FinFET made in the usual orientation on a (100) wafer, the fin sidewalls that form the channel are mainly (110) planes. What is the effect on mobility?
choices: Neither electron nor hole mobility changes
Compared with the (100) plane, hole mobility tends to rise and electron mobility tends to fall
Both electron and hole mobility increase greatly
finfet-050.explanation: Silicon mobility depends on crystal plane and current direction: on (110) surfaces hole mobility is higher (about twice) and electron mobility lower than on (100). In FinFETs most current flows along the sidewalls, an orientation that favors pMOS and penalizes nMOS; the nMOS deficit is offset with strain engineering. As a result, the nMOS-pMOS performance gap is smaller in FinFETs than in planar devices.
choiceNotes: Mobility does change with the crystal plane.
Correct. Holes tend to benefit and electrons to lose.
Electron mobility actually tends to drop on (110) planes.

finfet-051.question: For transistors with channels made of 2D materials such as MoS2, what is the main reason it is hard to deposit a uniform high-k gate dielectric by atomic layer deposition (ALD)?
choices: 2D materials are metals and react with the dielectric
Their surfaces have almost no dangling bonds, so there are few sites where ALD precursors can adsorb and start film growth
The surfaces of 2D materials are very rough, so ALD precursors cannot reach deep areas
finfet-051.explanation: Because 2D materials have no dangling bonds on their layer surfaces, they keep their mobility even below 1 nm thickness. The same property means ALD precursors hardly adsorb chemically on the surface, so films nucleate as islands at defects and grain boundaries and do not form thin, uniform dielectrics. Plasma-based methods tend to damage the layer, so approaches such as first forming a thin seed layer are being studied.
choiceNotes: MoS2 and similar materials are semiconductors, not metals.
Correct. The chemically inert surface is the cause.
The surface is atomically flat; roughness is not the cause.

finfet-052.question: Among 2D materials, why are transition metal dichalcogenides such as MoS2, rather than graphene, mainly studied as channels for logic transistors?
choices: Graphene has no bandgap, so a gate voltage cannot shut off the current well enough
Graphene is only stable at a thickness of 1 cm or more
Graphene is an insulator that does not conduct electricity
finfet-052.explanation: Graphene has very high mobility but no bandgap, so current flows even in the off state and the on/off current ratio stays small. Transition metal dichalcogenides such as MoS2 and WSe2 are semiconductors with a bandgap even as a single layer, and they work as transistors with channels about 0.65 nm thick. They are therefore studied as the next candidates for thinning channels beyond silicon nanosheets.
choiceNotes: Correct. Being unable to turn off is fatal for logic.
Graphene is stable even as a single atomic layer.
Graphene conducts electricity very well.

finfet-053.question: What is the main reason monolithic 3D integration can connect layers far more densely than 3D packaging that bonds separately made chips?
choices: The upper and lower layers are connected with solder bumps
The layers are connected with optical interconnects
The upper layer is built directly on the lower one and aligned by lithography, so layers can be connected with vias about the size of ordinary wiring vias
finfet-053.explanation: When chips or wafers are bonded, connection density is set by bonding alignment accuracy and connection size. In monolithic 3D integration, a thin semiconductor layer is formed or bonded on the first layer and the second transistor layer is made with lithographic alignment, so layers can be connected as finely as wiring vias. In exchange, the upper layer must be made at roughly 500 °C or below to avoid damaging the lower layer.
choiceNotes: Solder bumps have large pitches and are unsuited to dense connections.
Layers are connected with ordinary metal vias.
Correct. Alignment with lithographic accuracy is the reason.

finfet-054.question: In a CFET (complementary FET), which statement about connecting to the lower of the two stacked transistors is correct?
choices: The lower transistor has no gate, so only its source and drain need connections
Because the upper transistor sits directly above it, front-side connections must be routed around the upper device, and connecting to the lower device directly from the backside is being studied
The upper and lower transistors share all their sources and drains, so the lower device needs no separate connection
finfet-054.explanation: A CFET (complementary FET) stacks nMOS and pMOS vertically to shrink cell area. The gates and output can be shared, but each source must connect to a different supply (VDD and VSS). Reaching the lower device from the front side requires deep contacts routed around the upper transistor, crowding wiring in a small cell. Connecting directly to the lower device from the wafer backside, combined with backside power delivery, is therefore being studied; at IEDM 2023 Intel reported a working CFET inverter with direct backside contacts to the lower device.
choiceNotes: The lower transistor also has a gate, often shared with the upper one.
Correct. Access to the lower device becomes the wiring bottleneck.
Even in an inverter, the nMOS and pMOS sources connect to different supplies.
